entry: National intelligence agency of [[Israel]], formally the Institute for Intelligence and Special Operations. It was formed on December 13, 1949, as the Central Institute for Coordination at the recommendation of [[David Ben-Gurion]], and in 1951 it was placed in the prime minister's office. Because it reports to the prime minister rather than the Knesset, journalist Ronen Bergman has called it a "deep state." Mossad conducts intelligence collection, counterterrorism and covert operations, which have included many [[Assassination|assassination]] plots. It employs around 7,000 people, and its annual budget is around ₪10 billion (US$2.73 billion).

City in northern [[Iraq]], capital of Nineveh Governorate. It is the second-largest city in Iraq after [[Baghdad]] and sits on the banks of the [[Tigris]], across from the ruins of the ancient Assyrian city of Nineveh. Its strategic location made it a long-standing hub of commerce and travel in the region, and it is one of the historically significant cities of the [[Arab world]]. Arabs form the large majority of its population, alongside Kurds, Assyrians, Turkmens and Shabaks. [[Sunni Islam]] is the largest religion, with Christians and Yazidis also present. The surrounding region is rich in oil reserves, and the University of Mosul and its Medical College are among the Middle East's largest educational and research centers. The [[Islamic State]] seized the city in June 2014, and Iraqi forces backed by a U.S.-led coalition retook it in July 2017.

English rock band, formed in [[London]] in 1975. Lemmy Kilmister, its primary songwriter, was its only constant member. Most of its best-selling albums and singles featured drummer Phil Taylor and guitarist Fast Eddie Clarke. The band released 23 studio albums and is often considered a precursor to the new wave of British heavy metal. Kilmister insisted it was a rock and roll band, though it is most often classed as heavy metal and influenced thrash and speed metal. After Kilmister died of [[Arrhythmia|cardiac arrhythmia]] and [[Heart failure|congestive heart failure]], the remaining members confirmed that the band had disbanded.

Group of mostly nocturnal winged insects in the order [[Lepidoptera]]. Moths make up the vast majority of the order, with approximately 160,000 species, many not yet described. They are characterized by dark or dull patterned wings. They were once classified as suborder Heterocera, but that group is paraphyletic with respect to [[Butterfly|butterflies]], and neither subordinate taxon is used in modern classifications. Moths undergo complete [[Metamorphosis|metamorphosis]]. Adults generally lay eggs on or near plant foliage, and the [[Larva|larvae]], known as caterpillars, feed mostly on plant matter, although some species, such as *Eupithecia orichloris*, are carnivorous. Caterpillars often spin a [[Silk|silk]] cocoon before pupating, and the adult emerges from the [[Pupa|pupal]] skin. Moths are commonly thought to eat clothes, but only the larvae may consume natural fibers. They are found on all continents except Antarctica.

[[Albania|Albanian]]-Indian [[Catholic Church|Catholic]] nun and founder of the Missionaries of Charity. Born in Skopje, then part of the Ottoman Empire, she moved at 18 to Ireland to join the Sisters of Loreto and later lived most of her life in India. In 1950 she founded the Missionaries of Charity, initially to serve "the poorest of the poor" in the slums of [[Kolkata|Calcutta]]. By 2012 the congregation operated in over 133 countries, with more than 4,500 nuns running homes for people dying of [[HIV/AIDS]], [[Leprosy|leprosy]] and [[Tuberculosis|tuberculosis]]. She received the 1962 Ramon Magsaysay Peace Prize and the 1979 Nobel Peace Prize. Critics pointed to poor conditions and a lack of medical care or pain relief in her houses for the dying. She was canonized as [[Saint|Saint]] Teresa of Calcutta on September 4, 2016.

Female parent of a child. A woman may be considered a mother by giving birth, by raising a child who may not be her biological offspring, or by supplying her ovum for [[Fertilisation|fertilization]] in the case of gestational [[Surrogacy|surrogacy]]. A biological mother is the female genetic contributor to a child's creation, through [[Sexual intercourse|sexual intercourse]] or egg donation. An [[Adoption|adoptive]] mother becomes a parent through the legal process of adoption, and a stepmother is married to a child's existing parent but generally lacks the legal rights and responsibilities of a parent. In humans, a pregnant female gestates a fertilized ovum in the [[Uterus|uterus]], a process often lasting around nine months. Afterward the mother produces milk through lactation, and her breast milk supplies antibodies for the infant's [[Immune system|immune system]]. The verb "to mother" means to care for a child.

Humanoid creature of American folklore, said to have been seen near Point Pleasant, [[West Virginia]]. Sightings were reported from November 15, 1966, to December 15, 1967. Despite its name, the original sightings described [[Bird|avian]] features. Explanations include misidentified sandhill cranes or [[Heron|herons]], or barred owls. John Keel's 1975 book *The Mothman Prophecies* popularized the creature, linking it to [[Paranormal|paranormal]] events and the collapse of the Silver Bridge. A 2002 film adaptation starred Richard Gere, and an annual festival in Point Pleasant is devoted to the legend.

Internal state that propels individuals to engage in goal-directed behavior. It is often understood as a force that explains why people or animals initiate, continue or end a behavior. Motivational states are characterized by their direction, intensity and persistence. Intrinsic motivation comes from internal factors such as enjoyment and [[Curiosity|curiosity]], while extrinsic motivation is driven by external factors such as rewards and avoiding [[Punishment|punishment]]. Content theories, such as the hierarchy of needs, describe which internal factors motivate people, while process theories, such as expectancy theory and self-determination theory, examine the cognitive and emotional processes involved. The term comes from the Latin *movere* ("to move"). Motivation is studied in [[Psychology|psychology]], [[Neuroscience|neuroscience]] and [[Philosophy|philosophy]], and it affects educational success, work performance and athletic success.

Two- or three-wheeled [[Vehicle|motor vehicle]] steered by a handlebar from a saddle-style seat. The first internal combustion, [[Petroleum|petroleum]]-fueled motorcycle was the Daimler Reitwagen, built in 1885 by Gottlieb Daimler and Wilhelm Maybach in Germany. In 1894, Hildebrand & Wolfmüller became the first series-production motorcycle maker. In 2021 about 58.6 million new motorcycles were sold worldwide, compared with 66.7 million cars. In 2022 the top four producers by volume were [[Honda|Honda]], Yamaha, Kawasaki and Suzuki. Motorcycles are classified as street, off-road or dual-purpose, and many sub-types serve different purposes. According to the U.S. Department of Transportation, the 2024 motorcyclist fatality rate in the U.S. was 28.00 per 100 million vehicle miles traveled, almost 27 times the passenger-car occupant rate of 1.05.

American record label, founded by [[Berry Gordy|Berry Gordy Jr.]] as Tamla Records on January 12, 1959. Its name, a portmanteau of motor and town, became a nickname for [[Detroit]], where it was originally headquartered. As an African American-owned label, it achieved crossover success with white audiences, and its pop-influenced [[Soul music|soul]] style became known as the Motown sound. Between 1960 and 1969, 79 Motown songs reached the top ten of the Billboard Hot 100, and 21 reached No. 1. The label is now owned by [[Universal Music Group]].

Process by which an animal casts off parts of its body for some beneficial purpose. It is also called sloughing or shedding, and in many [[Invertebrate|invertebrates]] it is called *ecdysis*. Molting can shed the epidermis (skin), pelage (hair, feathers, fur or wool) or other external layers, and in [[Arthropod|arthropods]] the entire exoskeleton, including the wings of some insects. [[Bird|Birds]] molt at least once a year, replacing feathers gradually so they keep enough to regulate body temperature. Because [[Feather|feathers]] make up 4–12% of a bird's body weight, replacing them takes considerable energy, so molts often follow the breeding season while food is abundant. In some countries, commercial layer hens are force-molted to reinvigorate egg-laying, usually by withdrawing food for 7–14 days.

Snow-capped, dormant [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in easternmost [[Turkey]]. Greater Ararat, at 5,137 m (16,854 ft), is the highest peak in Turkey and the Armenian highlands. Friedrich Parrot, Khachatur Abovian and four others made the first recorded ascent in 1829. Although outside modern [[Armenia]], it is the principal national symbol of Armenia, is considered sacred by Armenians and appears on the national coat of arms. Europeans have called it Ararat since the [[Middle Ages]], identifying it with the biblical resting place of Noah's Ark.

Mountain on the Athos peninsula in northeastern [[Greece]], directly on the [[Aegean Sea]]. It is an important center of Eastern Orthodox monasticism. The mountain and most of the peninsula are an autonomous region governed by the monastic community, which is under the direct jurisdiction of the Ecumenical Patriarch of Constantinople. Greek law and religious tradition bar women from entering the area governed by the monastic community. Monastic traditions here date back to at least the 9th century. The monastic community was inscribed on the UNESCO [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] in 1988.

Dormant [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]], the highest mountain in Russia and Europe. It rises 5,642 m (18,510 ft) in the southern Russian republic of Kabardino-Balkaria and is the highest volcano in [[Eurasia]] as well as the highest peak of the [[Caucasus Mountains|Caucasus]]. Elbrus has two summits, both dormant volcanic domes: the western at 5,642 m and the eastern at 5,621 m (18,442 ft). The eastern summit was first climbed on July 10, 1829, by Circassian Khillar Khashirov, and the western in 1874 by a British expedition. The name may share a connection with Alborz, a mythical mountain in Zoroastrian tradition. It is also the tenth-most prominent peak in the world.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] on the east coast of [[Sicily]], [[Italy]]. It is one of the tallest active volcanoes in Europe and the tallest peak in Italy south of the Alps, at 3,403 m (11,165 ft) in September 2024, though its height varies with summit eruptions. It covers 1,190 sq km (459 sq mi) and is by far the largest of Italy's four active volcanoes, about two and a half times the height of the next largest, [[Mount Vesuvius]]. It is in an almost constant state of activity, and its fertile soils support vineyards and orchards on the lower slopes. The [[United Nations]] has designated it a Decade Volcano, and it was added to the UNESCO [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] in June 2013. In Greek mythology, [[Zeus]] trapped the monster Typhon beneath it, and the forges of [[Hephaestus]] were said to lie under it.

Highest mountain on Earth above [[Sea level|sea level]]. It lies in the Mahalangur Himal sub-range of the [[Himalayas]] and marks part of the China–[[Nepal]] border at its summit. Its height was measured in 2020 by Nepalese and Chinese authorities at 8,848.86 m (29,031 ft 8½ in). The standard route approaches from the southeast in Nepal, and the other from the north in China. Dangers include altitude sickness, weather, [[Avalanche|avalanches]] and the Khumbu Icefall, and as of May 2024, 340 people had died on the mountain. The first documented ascent was made in 1953 by [[Edmund Hillary]] and [[Tenzing Norgay]], via the Southeast Ridge. A Chinese team made the first reported ascent from the North Ridge on May 25, 1960.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] on the Japanese island of [[Honshu]], the highest mountain in [[Japan]]. It stands about 100 km (62 mi) southwest of [[Tokyo]], from which it is visible on clear days. Its symmetrical cone is snow-covered for about five months of the year, and it has long been a Japanese cultural icon, depicted often in art and photography. It last erupted from 1707 to 1708. Along with Mount Tate and Mount Haku, it is one of Japan's Three Holy Mountains. It was added to the UNESCO World Heritage List as a cultural site on June 22, 2013. UNESCO recognizes 25 sites of cultural interest within the mountain's locality, including the [[Shinto|Shinto]] shrine Fujisan Hongū Sengen Taisha.

Sacred mountain in Ngari Prefecture of the [[Tibet Autonomous Region]], [[China]]. Its peak rises to 6,638 m (21,778 ft) in the Gangdise Shan range of the Transhimalaya, on the western [[Tibetan Plateau]], near the trijunction of China, [[India]] and [[Nepal]]. Sacred in [[Buddhism]], [[Hinduism]], [[Jainism]] and Bon, the mountain draws pilgrims who trek to Lake Manasarovar and circumambulate the mountain. The Indus, Sutlej, Brahmaputra and Ghaghara rivers all rise in its vicinity. Nearby Lake Manasarovar is the highest freshwater lake in the world. No successful ascent has been recorded, and Chinese authorities prohibit climbing because of the mountain's religious significance.

Second-highest mountain in Africa, and namesake of [[Kenya]]. It lies about 150 km (90 mi) north-northeast of [[Nairobi]] and just 16.5 km south of the [[Equator|equator]]. Its highest peaks are Batian (5,199 m), Nelion (5,188 m) and Point Lenana (4,985 m). The area was gazetted as Mount Kenya National Park in 1949 and became a [[World Heritage Site|UNESCO World Heritage Site]] in 1997. The mountain was once covered by an ice cap, and its 11 small [[Glacier|glaciers]] are shrinking rapidly and may disappear by 2050. Its forests are an important water source for much of Kenya, and many alpine species, such as giant lobelias, are endemic. The Kikuyu believe the mountain is Ngai's throne on earth.

Dormant [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in [[Tanzania]], the highest mountain in Africa. Its highest point, Uhuru Peak, is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) above sea level, making it the highest free-standing mountain above sea level in the world. The German missionary Johannes Rebmann was the first European to report it, in 1848. Hans Meyer reached its highest summit in 1889. The mountain was incorporated into Kilimanjaro National Park in 1973. Seven established routes lead to Uhuru Peak, but its prominence poses a serious risk of altitude sickness. Its ice cap lost over 80% of its area in the 20th century and is projected to disappear entirely by the mid-21st century. The Chagga Kingdoms on its southern and eastern slopes were abolished in 1963 by [[Julius Nyerere]].

Highest mountain of mainland [[Australia]], in [[New South Wales]]. It rises 2,228 m (7,310 ft) on the Main Range of the Snowy Mountains in Kosciuszko National Park, part of the Australian Alps National Parks and Reserves. It is ranked 35th by topographic isolation. The Polish explorer Paweł (Paul) Edmund Strzelecki named it in 1840 after Tadeusz Kościuszko, because of its perceived resemblance to the Kościuszko Mound in [[Kraków]], [[Poland]]. Strzelecki reached the summit on March 12, 1840. Map errors confused it with neighboring Mount Townsend until a 1940 study by B. T. Dowd confirmed its status as Australia's highest summit.

Extensive massif in [[Greece]], on the border of Thessaly and Macedonia near the [[Aegean Sea]]. Its highest peak, Mytikas, rises 2,917.727 m (9,572.60 ft) and is the highest peak in Greece. The massif has 52 peaks and deep gorges. In [[Greek mythology]], Olympus is the home of the gods. It has been a national park since 1938, the first in Greece, and is also a World Biosphere Reserve. In July 2026 the wider area was inscribed on the UNESCO [[World Heritage Site|World Heritage List]] as a mixed site. Olympus remains the most popular hiking summit in Greece, usually approached from the town of Litochoro, about 100 km (62 mi) from [[Thessaloniki]].

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] at the northern end of [[Martinique]], an island in the [[Caribbean]]. Its most recent eruption was in 1932. The 1902 eruption destroyed the town of Saint-Pierre, killing 29,000 to 30,000 people in a few minutes, in the worst volcanic disaster of the 20th century. The main eruption, on May 8, 1902, left only three known survivors, one of whom, Ludger Sylbaris, had been in a poorly ventilated jail cell. The 1902 eruption took place within the Étang Sec [[Caldera|caldera]] and formed many [[Pyroclastic flow|pyroclastic flows]]. Further eruptions in 1929–1932 produced domes and pyroclastic flows, and the volcano remains under continuous watch by geophysicists and volcanologists.

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in the Zambales Mountains of [[Luzon]], [[Philippines]]. Its VEI-6 eruption on June 15, 1991, was the second-largest terrestrial eruption of the 20th century, after Novarupta in 1912. Early warnings led to the evacuation of tens of thousands of people, saving many lives. The eruption released roughly 10 billion tonnes (10 km³, or 2.4 cu mi) of magma and 20 million tonnes of SO₂. It ejected more particulate matter into the [[Stratosphere|stratosphere]] than any eruption since [[Krakatoa]] in 1883, forming a global sulfuric acid haze. Global temperatures dropped by about 0.5 °C (0.9 °F) in 1991–1993, and [[Ozone depletion|ozone depletion]] temporarily increased significantly. The volcano is about 87 km (54 mi) northwest of [[Manila]].

Active [[Stratovolcano|stratovolcano]] in the Cascade Range of the [[Pacific Northwest]], in the U.S. state of [[Washington (state)|Washington]]. At 14,406 ft (4,391 m) it is the highest mountain in Washington and the most topographically prominent mountain in the contiguous United States. It lies in Mount Rainier National Park, about 59 miles (95 km) south-southeast of [[Seattle]]. A U.S. Geological Survey report said that about 80,000 people and their homes are at risk in the volcano's lahar-hazard zones. Between 1947 and 2018, about 84 people died in [[Mountaineering|mountaineering]] accidents on the mountain.
